item.mechanism: Aging at intermediate temperatures (500–700 °C) enhances chemical ordering in the FCC matrix, creating perfectly ordered Ni3Al-like L12 domains with high antiphase boundary energy (APBE) and shear modulus, which promotes planar slip and severe strain localization, leading to ductile-to-brittle transition.
item.system: AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) aged at 600 °C for 20 h
item.operating_conditions: Isothermal aging at 600 °C for 20 h; tensile testing at room temperature; strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1
item.supporting_observation: The 600A alloy exhibits the lowest fracture elongation and impact energy, with L12 domains showing a Ni/Al ratio of ≈3:1 and significantly higher APBE compared to AC and 750A alloys.
item.scope_limits: Does not hold at low temperatures (<500 °C) or high temperatures (>750 °C) where ordering is less perfect or suppressed; not applicable to single-phase solid solution HEAs without LCO evolution.
item.alternatives_considered: Classical temper embrittlement driven by grain boundary segregation of impurities (e.g., S, Bi, P) or brittle phase precipitation along grain boundaries.
quotes: Aging within the embrittlement‐prone regime enhances chemical ordering, increases the density of ordered domains, and induces jagged PBs, collectively triggering plastic instability and the ductile−to−brittle transition.

Specifically, the L1 2 domains in the 600A alloy display a significantly lower Al content, and the atomic ratio of Ni/Al is ≈3:1, which keeps the Ni/Al ratio of a perfectly L1 2 ‐ordered Ni 3 Al structure.
Aging at 600 °C induces enhanced ordering with higher APBE, which intensifies this planarity, leading to pronounced strain localization and unsustainable working hardening.

item.mechanism: The formation of jagged, low-coherency phase boundaries (PBs) during aging acts as strong barriers to dislocation transmission, causing dislocation pile-ups and high stress concentrations at PB tips, which nucleates microcracks and accelerates brittle failure.
item.operating_conditions: Aging at 600 °C for 20 h; deformation under tensile stress; observation of PB morphology via TEM and TKD
item.supporting_observation: The 600A alloy displays jagged PBs with high-resistance Interface I segments, leading to severe dislocation pile-ups and tearing decohesion cracking along the PBs in fracture cross-sections.
item.scope_limits: Not observed in the as-cast (AC) state with smooth interfaces or in the 750A alloy where PBs become smoother or develop ductile transition zones; mechanism competes with the ductile recovery at higher temperatures.
item.alternatives_considered: Grain boundary embrittlement via impurity segregation; smooth phase boundaries that allow continuous dislocation slip.
quotes: Aging within the embrittlement‐prone regime enhances chemical ordering, increases the density of ordered domains, and induces jagged PBs, collectively triggering plastic instability and the ductile−to−brittle transition.
When these slip bands impinge upon the jagged PBs, especially the high‐resistance Interface I segments, dislocation pile‐ups concentrate shear stresses at the serration tips.

item.mechanism: Aging at higher temperatures (750 °C) reduces the order degree of L12 domains (making them off-stoichiometric and weakly ordered), which promotes dislocation cross-slip and multiple slip system activation, leading to a brittle-to-ductile recovery via a glide plane self-hardening effect.
item.system: AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 EHEA aged at 750 °C for 20 h
item.operating_conditions: Isothermal aging at 750 °C for 20 h; tensile testing; observation of dislocation networks and L12 domain structure
item.supporting_observation: The 750A alloy shows a Ni/Al ratio of ≈2:1 in L12 domains, complex dislocation networks, and high fracture elongation (nearly three times that of 600A), indicating restored ductility.
item.scope_limits: Does not apply to the 600A regime where ordering is perfect; the mechanism relies on the specific off-stoichiometric composition of L12 domains at this temperature.
item.alternatives_considered: Continued strengthening via perfect ordering (as in 600A) which would maintain brittleness; grain coarsening which is not observed.
quotes: In contrast, aging outside this regime suppresses excessive ordering and promotes the formation of ductile interphase transition zones, facilitating a brittle−to−ductile recovery.
Crucially, these L1 2 domains are off‐stoichiometric and only weakly ordered, which significantly alters the deformation behavior of the FCC(L1 2 ) matrix.

item.mechanism: The dissolution of Cr-rich particles (CRPs) at phase boundaries at 750 °C creates a CRP-free zone (ductile transition zone) with lower hardness, which enhances deformation compatibility, reduces stress concentration, and prevents crack initiation at phase boundaries.
item.operating_conditions: Aging at 750 °C for 20 h; thermal exposure allowing Cr diffusion; nanoindentation and TKD analysis of PB regions
item.supporting_observation: The 750A alloy exhibits a clean area adjacent to PBs lacking CRPs, lower GND density in the B2 edge area, and intact PBs in fracture cross-sections, contrasting with the CRP-embedded B2 phase in AC and 600A alloys.
item.scope_limits: Only occurs at temperatures where CRPs are thermodynamically unstable (e.g., 750 °C); not observed at 600 °C where CRPs are stable and enhance hardening.
item.alternatives_considered: Retention of CRPs at PBs which causes pinning and stress concentration; precipitation of new brittle phases.
quotes: The other key feature in the 750A alloy is the unique B2 edge region near B2/FCC(L1 2 ) PBs, which notably lacks CRPs, namely the CRPs‐free zone.
This dissolution process ceases once the Cr concentration in the B2 matrix reaches the equilibrium solubility at this temperature, thereby promoting and stabilizing the CRP‐free zone within B2.

This is due to the absence of CRPs strengthening in the B2 edge areas, allowing deformation dislocation to transfer through PBs more easily, which enhances deformation compatibility and reduces stress concentration around the PBs.

item.mechanism: The synergistic effect of enhanced LCO-induced planar slip and jagged PBs creates a coupled embrittlement pathway where localized slip bands terminate at low-transmissivity PBs, causing rapid stress rise and crack nucleation.
item.operating_conditions: Aging at 600 °C; tensile deformation; analysis of slip bands and PB interactions via TEM and TKD
item.supporting_observation: The 600A alloy shows single-orientation planar slip bands that impinge on jagged PBs, leading to dislocation pile-ups and microcrack nucleation at PB tips, distinct from the uniform deformation in 750A.
item.scope_limits: Specific to the coupled evolution of LCO and PBs in this multiphase EHEA; not applicable to single-phase alloys or conventional alloys where GB segregation dominates.
item.alternatives_considered: Classical intergranular fracture due to GB cohesion loss; uniform plastic flow without strain localization.
quotes: The synergistic embrittlement resulting from L1 2 ‐induced planar slip and serrated, low‐coherency PBs is illustrated in Figure 5A,C .
Planar slip is funneled into narrow channels that terminate at serrated, low‐transmissivity PBs, leading to stress localization and crack formation.
Once it exceeds the local yield or decohesion threshold, microcracks nucleate and propagate along these stress concentrators, producing brittle failure.

item.mechanism: The thermal evolution of LCOs and PBs is reversible; applying appropriate heat treatments can recover the ductility of an embrittled alloy, suggesting potential for recyclability and the design of temperature-sensitive safety devices.
item.operating_conditions: Aging at 600 °C followed by aging at 750 °C or higher; thermal cycling within the 500–750 °C window
item.supporting_observation: The ductile-brittle-ductile transition is observed across the temperature range, with the 750A alloy recovering ductility lost in the 600A state; the authors propose using this window for 'temperature fuses'.
item.scope_limits: Requires specific temperature windows (500–750 °C); the reversibility is demonstrated for this specific alloy system and may not transfer to all HEAs without similar LCO/PB dynamics.
item.alternatives_considered: Permanent degradation of properties due to irreversible phase decomposition or grain coarsening.
quotes: Importantly, the ductile−brittle transition exhibits thermally reversible behavior, suggesting that this alloy system holds promise for recyclability and sustainable material applications.
By applying appropriate heat treatments, the embrittled alloy can fully recover its high strength and ductility, enabling repeated reuse without performance degradation.

Moreover, leveraging the well‐defined embrittlement window, one can engineer HEA rupture discs, shear pins, or over‐temperature disconnects that fail safely and predictably at fire‐relevant temperatures (≈500–600 °C).

item.mechanism: DFT calculations indicate that reducing Al content in L12 domains and increasing Ni/Al ratio to 3:1 significantly increases the antiphase boundary energy (APBE) and shear modulus, which raises the critical shear stress for dislocation motion and promotes brittleness.
item.operating_conditions: Computational simulation using DFT; modeling of Ni1.5Al and Ni2Al supercells with Fe, Co, Cr doping
item.supporting_observation: DFT results show that as the Ni:Al ratio changes from 2:1 to 3:1, the APBE increases substantially, correlating with the higher order degree and brittleness observed in the 600A alloy.
item.scope_limits: Based on theoretical models of L12 domains; assumes specific doping effects of Fe, Co, Cr which may vary in other alloy systems.
item.alternatives_considered: Lower APBE and shear modulus associated with off-stoichiometric L12 domains (2:1 ratio) which facilitate ductility.
quotes: More significantly, as the atomic ratio of Ni: Al changes from nearly 2:1 to 3:1, the APBE also increases substantially.
Collectively, these findings suggest that the L1 2 domains in the 600A alloy exhibit a higher APBE and an expanded shear modulus, compared to those in the AC and 750A alloys.
The DFT results in Figure 3H reveal that a reduction in Al content in the L1 2 domains leads to a significant increase in shear modulus.

item.mechanism: The presence of Cr-rich particles (CRPs) in the B2 phase acts as a pinning force for dislocations, but when combined with jagged PBs, it exacerbates stress concentration and promotes brittle failure, whereas their absence at PBs facilitates ductile recovery.
item.operating_conditions: Tensile deformation; observation of dislocation-CRP interactions via TEM; aging treatments at 600 °C and 750 °C
item.supporting_observation: In 600A, CRPs in the B2 phase combined with jagged PBs lead to high-density dislocation accumulation and cracking; in 750A, the CRP-free zone at PBs allows dislocations to glide easily, mitigating stress concentration.
item.scope_limits: The pinning effect is beneficial in the AC state with smooth PBs but detrimental when PBs become jagged; the mechanism depends on the spatial distribution of CRPs relative to PBs.
item.alternatives_considered: CRPs acting solely as strengthening precipitates without considering their interaction with PB topology; smooth PBs allowing slip transfer despite CRPs.
quotes: Within the B2 phase, numerous arrow‐shaped dislocations are observed around the CRPs (yellow arrows in Figure 4A(iii) ), indicating that these CRPs impose a strong pinning force to hinder dislocation movement.
High‐density dislocations are observed to accumulate at the jagged PBs, which indicates high stress concentration (Figure 4B(iii) ).

Notably, we observed that dislocations glide easily across the regions lacking CRPs around the B2/FCC(L1 2 ) PBs (indicated by the white arrow in Figure 4C(iii) ), while these gliding dislocations become pinned and entangled upon encountering the CRPs in the B2 phase.
